title: The Politics of Human Sexuality

jokes.text: laser projecting a burning pelvis onto the ceiling. A laser!
jokes.setup: Annie is enthusiastically describing her contributions to the STD awareness fair — sketch artist, improv troupe — normal event-planning items
jokes.punchline: ...and a laser projecting a burning pelvis onto the ceiling. The Dean's excited repetition of 'A laser!' treats the most absurd element as the highlight
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity from normal event items to a burning-pelvis laser is a solid cold-open joke. The Dean's enthusiasm for the wrong detail is good character work. Not transcendent but well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Your mother's so positive, she tested positive for chlamydia.

jokes.text: Well, this isn't gonna be your mother's sexually transmitted disease awareness fair.
jokes.setup: Dean is hyping the STD fair
jokes.punchline: Using the classic 'not your mother's X' idiom applied to an STD fair — the phrase implies a hip upgrade to something inherently unglamorous
jokes.explanation: Competent application of a familiar formula to an absurd topic. The Dean's oblivious pomposity is on-brand but the joke itself is fairly predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The STD awareness fair slogan is 'Catch Knowledge, Not Diseases.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's actually pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Thank you! I spent all morning coming up with it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, I have notes.

jokes.text: Oh, STD fair, guys. Catch knowledge.
jokes.setup: Annie is enthusiastically promoting the fair to her study group, mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, oddly corporate slogan 'Catch knowledge' delivered with Annie's relentless pep is funny in its incongruity with the subject matter
jokes.explanation: The slogan itself is brilliant economy — a two-word catchphrase that parodies public health messaging while perfectly capturing Annie's overachiever personality. It becomes a running gag, earning rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You reference movies in literally every conversation. Can't you just talk normally?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's like asking Denzel Washington to stop being Denzel Washington.

jokes.text: You stick to quotin' movie lines. I'll stick to sports.
jokes.setup: Jeff claims he's trying to reduce his pop-cultural referencing; Troy challenges him to basketball
jokes.punchline: Troy's crisp division of labor — Jeff's whole identity is movie quotes, Troy's is sports — delivered as a matter of settled fact
jokes.explanation: Good character-defining shorthand. Troy's confidence is funny but the joke is fairly light — it's more setup for the Jeff-Troy basketball subplot than a standalone laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: Well, 'secretary' is a pretty degrading term.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: I prefer 'officey things person.'

jokes.text: No, it doesn't! And it won't be.
jokes.setup: Jeff responds to Troy's challenge to play basketball with 'Sounds fun'
jokes.punchline: Troy's instant, emphatic, two-pronged rebuttal — present AND future tense — rejects even the possibility of fun with total certainty
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic economy. The parallel tense construction ('doesn't... won't be') packs a lot of competitive aggression into five words. Troy's hyper-competitive nature shines. The structure is tighter than it looks.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, did correcting the title make it less sexist? Because I'm pretty sure the job is still the same.

jokes.text: "Secretary" is a little degrading to women. / I help the dean do officey things. / Oh, gender saved.
jokes.setup: Dean introduces Sabrina as his 'secretary'; Jeff objects on feminist grounds
jokes.punchline: Sabrina's replacement — 'I help the dean do officey things' — is demonstrably worse, and Jeff's flat 'Oh, gender saved' punctuates how hollow the correction was
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, gender saved' is sharp, perfectly timed satire of performative linguistic sensitivity. The three-step structure (objection → worse correction → deflating punchline) is well-engineered. Jeff's sarcasm is exactly right for his character.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We've had another incident. Three toilet seats have gone missing from the faculty bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Dean, that's terrible. Do we know who took them?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, that's the thing. Security footage shows they're being stolen by a highly organized ring of toilet seat thieves who are using them to construct an elaborate throne in the air vents.

jokes.text: My casual friend and I are gonna have a non-romantic breakfast if you'd like to join us.
jokes.setup: Jeff is talking to Sabrina, clearly trying to flirt or make an impression
jokes.punchline: The labored, over-qualified description of what is obviously a date attempt — 'casual friend,' 'non-romantic' — reveals Jeff's practiced nonchalance as performance
jokes.explanation: Very Jeff Winger — the smooth veneer is so thick it becomes transparently insecure. 'Non-romantic' is the tell. Good character-specific comedy that rewards knowing Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We have a toilet seat theft problem in the faculty bathroom. I've decided to install hidden cameras in all the stalls.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Dean, that's illegal.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Not if I'm also using the bathroom. Then it's just me enjoying my own privacy.

jokes.text: I want hidden cameras in every stall. Problem solved.
jokes.setup: Someone points out the women's bathroom toilet seats keep getting stolen; Dean says 'Sabrina, take a note.'
jokes.punchline: His solution to toilet seat theft is hidden cameras in bathroom stalls — a wildly disproportionate and creepy response delivered with total administrative confidence
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures the Dean's combination of institutional authority and deeply questionable judgment. The brisk 'Problem solved' makes it funnier — he sees no issue whatsoever. Strong character-comedy that reveals institutional dysfunction.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What does this fortune cookie say? 'Your future is cloudy, but treatment is available.'

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Oh, that's from our STD fair! I'm so proud of that marketing campaign.

jokes.text: "You will get aids." / Flip it over. / "Unless you go to the STD fair."  / I wrote that. / Congratu... horrible!
jokes.setup: Dean proudly reads the fortune cookie: 'You will get aids.' — a horrifying standalone statement
jokes.punchline: The flip side provides the STD-fair plug, completing a dark marketing scheme. Jeff's truncated 'Congratu... horrible!' captures both the acknowledgment and disgust simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The fortune cookie structure is perfect delivery for a two-part dark punchline. 'You will get aids' as a standalone line is a great cold shock, and then flipping it reveals a logic that's simultaneously clever marketing and deeply wrong. Jeff's portmanteau reaction — 'Congratu... horrible!' — is quotable, perfectly compressed, and shows the writers trusting a neologism. High originality, tight structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, I want to congratulate you on—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, no. I don't.

jokes.text: And she is super smart, if you know what I mean.
jokes.setup: Pierce tells Jeff he has a new girlfriend and says she's 'super smart'
jokes.punchline: 'If you know what I mean' implies something sexual about being 'super smart' — the innuendo is muddy and self-undermining, which is the joke about Pierce's obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Pierce's muddy innuendo is a character beat — the joke IS that his implication doesn't quite land, which is true to his character. Mildly funny but relatively low-craft.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My girlfriend is so smart.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, Pierce, we all know what you mean.

jokes.text: Unfortunately, I always know what you mean.
jokes.setup: Pierce says his new girlfriend is 'super smart, if you know what I mean'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's weary 'Unfortunately, I always know what you mean' — perfectly laconic, implying he's been subjected to Pierce's muddy innuendo for too long
jokes.explanation: Superb economy. 'Unfortunately' does all the work — it concedes understanding while expressing total dread. This is Jeff at his best: the straight man who's smarter than everyone and exhausted by it. Very few words, big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, a relationship is like fishing. You cast your line out there, wait for a bite, and when you feel that tug, you reel her in real hard. Sometimes she flops around a lot, and you gotta keep reeling no matter what. Eventually she stops moving, and that's when you know you got her.

jokes.text: When you catch a big fish, you want to stuff her and put her on the mantle.
jokes.setup: Pierce is excitedly describing his new girlfriend
jokes.punchline: The fishing metaphor applied to a woman — 'stuff her and put her on the mantle' — is deeply unreconstructed but played as innocent enthusiasm, which is the Pierce joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce obliviousness — the metaphor's objectifying implications sail completely over his head. Character-consistent but not especially inventive for the show's standards.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's not the basketball, Troy. It's your eyes. The way they light up when you're playing. Like two suns burning in the gymnasium of my heart.

jokes.text: She's an escort. / Oh... / Some mysteries solve themselves, don't they?
jokes.setup: 'What does she do?' — group expects any normal answer
jokes.punchline: 'She's an escort' lands as a collective 'Oh...' moment; Jeff's follow-up connects it back to Pierce's 'big fish' boasting without saying so explicitly
jokes.explanation: 'Some mysteries solve themselves' is an elegant, low-key line that captures the group's collective epiphany. Jeff's delivery would be perfectly flat. Good structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My girlfriend is a stripper.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, that explains the pole in your bedroom.

jokes.text: Taking a call girl to an STD fair. There's a joke here.
jokes.setup: Pierce announces he's taking Doreen (the escort) to Annie's STD fair
jokes.punchline: Jeff meta-acknowledges the joke's existence without making it, which IS the joke — both commenting on and embodying restraint
jokes.explanation: Smart, self-aware writing. Jeff notes the comedic potential without exploiting it, which is funnier than the punchline itself would have been. Very Community — the show's meta-awareness deployed character-specifically. 'There's a joke here' is perfectly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is the part where I should make a joke about how she's going to an STD fair, but I'm not going to finish it.

jokes.text: Is there a pill that makes the word 'no' clearer?
jokes.setup: Pierce pressures Jeff to 'rustle up a honey' for a double date, ignoring Jeff's clear 'no'
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames Pierce's density as a pharmacological problem — implying the issue is reception, not transmission
jokes.explanation: Very sharp. The pharmaceutical framing recontextualizes Pierce's obtuseness as a medical condition, which is both a great insult and contextually appropriate given the STD fair setting. High economy, strong originality, very Jeff-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I wish women came with rejection letters. Like, 'Dear Jeff, thank you for your interest, but we've decided to pursue other candidates. Sincerely, every woman ever.'

jokes.text: Well, I guess it is pretty short notice. Probably couldn't get a date anyway. / I'm sure you're right. [group reacts]
jokes.setup: Pierce baits Jeff by suggesting he 'probably couldn't get a date anyway'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's completely flat 'I'm sure you're right' — refusing to take the bait — followed by the group's audible 'Oooohh' as if he'd been burned anyway
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between Jeff's non-reaction and the group's reaction — they treat his deadpan as a devastating comeback. The 'Oooohh' is funnier BECAUSE Jeff didn't actually do anything. Good ensemble timing.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, did you say crabs? Like the food?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh. Because I was gonna say, I had some crab last week and I got really sick.

jokes.text: Maybe it has something to do with crabs. They're like a food, but they're also a disease.
jokes.setup: Group is pondering what joke could exist about taking a call girl to an STD fair
jokes.punchline: Britta's earnest, belated, and incorrect attempt to identify the joke — connecting 'crabs' as the bridge between sex work and STDs — demonstrates her complete lack of comedic instinct
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta — she tries to engage with humor the way someone who has studied humor would, missing the point. 'They're like a food, but they're also a disease' is delivered as genuine insight. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've been with way more women than you, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, Pierce. You've been with a lot of women. You've been with *a lot* of women. Most of them professionals.

jokes.text: Well, I don't know the precise date, Pierce, because I'm not you, so there's no receipt.
jokes.setup: Pierce asks when Jeff last 'scored,' implying he's on a dry spell
jokes.punchline: Jeff's comeback implies Pierce pays for sex (connecting to the escort revelation) — the 'receipt' reframes Pierce's question as an admission about himself
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The 'receipt' callback to Pierce's escort girlfriend is perfectly constructed — it disarms Pierce's attack by turning it into a self-indictment, it's completely unexpected, and it's delivered in Jeff's most economical register. 'I'm not you, so there's no receipt' — the negation structure makes the insult land harder. Highly quotable, strong originality, flawless economy. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why did the crab never share his pearls? Because he was shellfish!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: ...I've been waiting all day to say that.

jokes.text: No. This is. 'Don't eat the crab dip.' Yay-yay!
jokes.setup: Britta asks 'What is this, some kind of joke?' while looking at a flyer; Jeff says 'No'
jokes.punchline: Annie triumphantly presents the crab dip sign as a joke she's written — 'Yay-yay!' punctuates her disproportionate pride in a middling pun
jokes.explanation: The joke within the joke — Annie's pun is weak, but her 'Yay-yay!' celebration sells it as Annie-specific character comedy. The layered structure (Britta asks about jokes, Annie answers with one) is tidy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What is that sound? It sounds like... a fair?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no, no, no. The STD awareness fair. I completely forgot.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know what? I bet the STDs are really upset about this. I mean, think about it—they finally get some attention, and it's all negative. Nobody's throwing them a parade.

jokes.text: That's the sound of STDs screaming, 'No! Stop being so aware of us!'
jokes.setup: Dean is celebrating the fair setup with Annie, hearing ambient noise
jokes.punchline: He anthropomorphizes STDs as defeated enemies fleeing from awareness — the grandiose absurdity is entirely characteristic
jokes.explanation: The Dean's self-aggrandizing theatrical worldview projected onto STDs is a fun bit. The image of frightened diseases screaming is absurdly vivid. Dean-specific and funny, though not the episode's sharpest.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: My father used to call it 'the Dean.' He'd say, 'Cover up your Dean,' or 'Stop touching your Dean in public.' I didn't realize until much later what he was talking about.

jokes.text: I was voted most likely to succeed at my rehab clinic.
jokes.setup: Dean compliments Annie on her hard work at the fair
jokes.punchline: Annie's response reframes 'success' through the lens of rehab — a casually dropped reference to her darker backstory that she delivers with complete pride
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. This line does double duty: it's a callback to Annie's established backstory AND it reframes 'most likely to succeed' in a way that reveals both her genuine pride and her obliviousness to how it sounds. The word 'clinic' instead of 'center' or 'program' adds specificity. Very Annie Edison — overachieving in every context, including recovery. Strong candidate for top jokes in episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Annie, don't worry. I've been in this situation before. When I was younger, I had a very active modeling career myself. Very active. Sometimes too active, if you know what I mean. I'm talking about the modeling, of course. Though there was also a lot of... other activity. Very flexible. Very... limber.

jokes.text: ...what my dad called a Jimmy Carter.
jokes.setup: Dean is asking Annie to demonstrate putting a condom on an anatomically correct model
jokes.punchline: His father's euphemism for a penis is 'a Jimmy Carter' — inexplicably specific, deeply weird, and characteristic of the Dean's archaic social register
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes for pure originality. 'Jimmy Carter' as a penis euphemism is so specific, so inexplicable, and so perfect for the Dean — a man whose upbringing clearly involved extremely peculiar conversations. The specificity of a presidential name (not just any president, but Carter specifically) is the key. No other character on any show would have this line. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey, it's Jeff. Yeah, the guy from last night. Look, I know this is forward, but I was thinking we could grab dinner sometime. Yeah? Great. So I'll pick you up at, uh... your place. The address you gave me. Which I definitely have written down somewhere. Actually, you know what? Just tell me your address again. And also... what was your name again?

jokes.text: Don't worry, not a real one. No, it's an anatomically correct model, you know. But trust me, eyes closed, you can't tell the difference.
jokes.setup: Annie expresses uncertainty about doing the condom demonstration; Dean reassures her it's not a real one
jokes.punchline: 'But trust me, eyes closed, you can't tell the difference' — the Dean's reassurance crosses directly into inappropriate overshare/personal testimony
jokes.explanation: Perfectly executed cringe comedy. The Dean's attempt to reassure Annie devolves into what is clearly personal experience with the model. The escalating overshare structure ('not real... anatomically correct... eyes closed') works as a triple-beat with the punchline at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jeff, your contact list has categories for women. 'Backup,' 'Instagram models,' 'Britta's friends I can date,' and... 'Mom.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's just organization.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your mom is listed under 'Do Not Call.'

jokes.text: Annie's reaction beat — silent horror after 'eyes closed, you can't tell the difference'
jokes.setup: Dean makes his disturbing reassurance about the model
jokes.punchline: Annie's silent 'Okay' — the horrified acceptance of someone who has just learned too much and must press forward anyway
jokes.explanation: The 'Okay' that follows is funny precisely because it's the smallest possible response to the Dean's revelation. Annie's willingness to absorb horror and move on is character-consistent. Works as a beat to close the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, who's 'mommy' in your phone?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not my mother.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not judging. Well, I am, but not about that.

jokes.text: What do you mean, do I know your name? What kind of a question is that? Of course I know. Well, if I answer now, you'll never learn a valuable lesson about trust, Jennifer. Crap!
jokes.setup: Jeff is making outgoing calls trying to find a date; we realize mid-call he doesn't know the woman's name
jokes.punchline: His attempt to bluff — 'you'll never learn a valuable lesson about trust' — is immediately torpedoed by guessing 'Jennifer' and being wrong
jokes.explanation: Great escalating structure. The philosophical gambit ('valuable lesson about trust') to cover not knowing her name is brilliantly pompous and very Jeff. The immediate 'Jennifer. Crap!' deflates it perfectly. The scene efficiently establishes the phone book subplot while being consistently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jeff, your contact list is organized by how attractive you find each person, with a sub-category for 'might sleep with me.' That's sociopathic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's efficient!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's evil.

jokes.text: "Car wash redhead. Tube top, REM Concert." / "Juror number six." That sounds aboveboard.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy browse Jeff's phone contacts, which describe women by circumstance rather than name
jokes.punchline: 'Juror number six' — Troy's dry 'That sounds aboveboard' is perfect deadpan response to the obvious implication that Jeff may have pursued a juror during a trial
jokes.explanation: The phone book conceit is funny on its own (each entry is a snapshot of Jeff's shallow past), but 'That sounds aboveboard' applied to 'Juror number six' is the standout — the specific legal/ethical implication packed into deadpan understatement. Troy's straight-man delivery makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, is that why they call it a banana hammock?

jokes.text: At least you have 'mommy' in here. / It's not my mom. / Dude, not cool. / You saying 'dude' is not cool.
jokes.setup: Troy notes 'mommy' is in Jeff's phone as if it's wholesome; Jeff's correction implies it's a woman he's dating
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'Dude, not cool' is immediately deflected by Jeff pointing out that Troy saying 'dude' isn't cool either — a quick pivot that escapes the judgment
jokes.explanation: Two-step joke that works well. The 'mommy' revelation is funny; the 'dude, not cool' / 'you saying dude is not cool' exchange has a nice rhythm and shows Jeff's reflex to deflect any criticism.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: A virgin in 2013? Girl, you're like a unicorn!

jokes.text: "Hot blonde, Spanish class"? / You're welcome.
jokes.setup: Abed reads another entry from Jeff's phone book — 'Hot blonde, Spanish class'
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately claims credit — 'You're welcome' — implying he is the hot blonde Jeff met in Spanish class, which is both a callback to their shared class and a joke about Troy's self-image
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. 'You're welcome' from Troy reading that entry is unexpected, confident, and reveals a lot about how Troy sees himself while also being a great absurdist beat. Very high economy — nine words including setup. Troy's casual self-regard is perfectly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm not a virgin! I've had sex. Multiple times. With different people.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, okay, there was the incident behind the Costco, but that was consensual.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And yes, there were witnesses, but they were very supportive.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The police were just doing their job.

jokes.text: This is the phone book of a man in his 20s. The women literally have no identities.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy are marveling at Jeff's phone; Jeff is on the phone trying to remember names
jokes.punchline: Britta's feminist critique is completely correct — which makes Jeff's subsequent 'You're right. I can't believe I haven't seen it before now.' even funnier as performative capitulation
jokes.explanation: Britta's observation is on-brand and correct, but the joke itself is fairly predictable in this context. Jeff's instant 'you're right' response below is funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I saw Harvey Keitel's penis in The Piano.

jokes.text: You're right. I can't believe I haven't seen it before now. / Whatever. I'm gonna go study with Shirley. / Well, I'll be here... Rethinking my way of life.
jokes.setup: Britta makes a valid feminist critique of Jeff's phone book; Jeff immediately 'agrees'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's instant, theatrical self-examination ('Rethinking my way of life') is transparently hollow — he's doing just enough to make Britta leave, then drops it the moment she does
jokes.explanation: 'Rethinking my way of life' delivered as the most low-energy introspective statement possible, then contrasted with immediately calling 'mommy,' is a perfect capsule of Jeff's character. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I need to practice my negotiation skills.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'll just commit tax fraud. That'll help.

jokes.text: Britta, do you have a banana? / This is an anatomically correct model I'll be handling. / Real... watchamacallits... are nothing like bananas!
jokes.setup: Annie tells the group she needs to practice putting a condom on a model; Shirley suggests using a banana
jokes.punchline: Annie's horrified correction — 'Real... watchamacallits... are nothing like bananas!' — reveals she has opinions about anatomical accuracy while also being deeply avoidant of saying the word
jokes.explanation: 'Watchamacallits' as Annie's euphemism is perfect character work — she can speak knowledgeably about anatomy while still being incapable of using the clinical term. The contradiction between her confident assertion and her verbal avoidance is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, it's okay. I went through a dry spell once. Lasted seven years.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Seven years?!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, eight if you count my second marriage.

jokes.text: Have you never seen one? / being a virgin in this day and age is something to be proud of. You're like a unicorn.
jokes.setup: Annie's strong reaction to the banana suggestion implies she has limited experience with the subject
jokes.punchline: 'You're like a unicorn' — Shirley's well-meaning but backhanded compliment framing virginity as mythological
jokes.explanation: Solid joke. 'You're like a unicorn' works because it sounds complimentary but implies Annie doesn't exist in the modern world. Shirley's oblivious earnestness is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Background performer
dialogue.line: Oh no, I caught gonorrhea!

dialogue.speaker: Background performer
dialogue.line: Why would you give me herpes at a carnival?!

dialogue.speaker: Background performer
dialogue.line: I won chlamydia! This is the worst prize ever!

jokes.text: I had relations with my high school boyfriend. We did it to Madonna's Erotica on the floor of his walk-in closet. But he wouldn't let me look at it. And he cried after. And during. He's gay now. I think he was gay then.
jokes.setup: Annie defends herself against the 'unicorn' characterization by describing her sexual experience
jokes.punchline: Each additional detail makes the story progressively sadder/funnier: the closet floor → wouldn't let her look → crying during and after → he's gay now → 'I think he was gay then' — the final line being the most devastating understatement
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the series. The escalation structure is masterful — each detail is worse than the last, and each one could be the punchline but isn't. 'He's gay now' would be enough, but the kicker 'I think he was gay then' is devastatingly precise. It's also deeply character-specific: only Annie would recount this story with complete matter-of-fact composure while trying to prove she's not a virgin. The Madonna's Erotica/walk-in closet combination is specific enough to feel real. This genuinely earns 9+ comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Well, Sabrina enjoys competitive badminton, the smell of copper pennies, and she has a complicated relationship with the concept of Tuesdays.

jokes.text: So you, uh, you never seen one when you were growing up? Like, you know, on the Internet, in a picture, or Harvey Keitel's?
jokes.setup: Group trying to establish how inexperienced Annie actually is with male anatomy
jokes.punchline: 'Harvey Keitel's' — Shirley's escalating list of ways to have encountered anatomy ends with a specific celebrity known for full-frontal nudity, which reveals far more about Shirley than Annie
jokes.explanation: The joke pivots from Annie to Shirley — the specific reference to Harvey Keitel (known for nude scenes in The Piano, Bad Lieutenant, etc.) tells us something unexpected about Shirley's viewing history. Good specificity, good character reveal, solid structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, horses are like... they're majestic creatures that force us to confront our own mortality. When you're riding a horse, you're not just moving through space, you're moving through time itself. It's almost spiritual.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: Do you even know what horses eat?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course. Freedom. Horses eat freedom, and that's why they're so beautiful.

jokes.text: I actually have no problem with that. / I think I could do that.
jokes.setup: Annie says they need to break into the dean's office to practice with the model; she expects resistance
jokes.punchline: Britta and Abed both immediately and cheerfully sign up — their total lack of moral hesitation is funnier than any objection would have been
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble character beat. The joke is in the reversal — Annie braces for pushback, gets enthusiastic compliance. Britta's anarchic streak and Abed's matter-of-fact competence both show through.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, Jeff, you've really outdone yourself this time. She's way out of your league.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Don't worry about it, kid. What you're going through is a dry spell. From my experience, they don't last any more than 12, 13 years.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is trying to console Jeff about not having a date, framing it as a 'dry spell'
jokes.punchline: 'They don't last any more than 12, 13 years' — Pierce's reassurance reveals his own longest dry spell was over a decade
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed self-own. Pierce's attempt to minimize Jeff's dry spell only works because Pierce's reference point is 12-13 years — which is the actual punchline. The casual 'from my experience' makes it land harder. Classic Pierce: obliviously revealing his own pathos while trying to help.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, I guess I'm taking home an STD fair prize.

jokes.text: Step right up. Get a prize, not an STD. Oh, no, syphilis. Please, please, no, syphilis. Ow, it burns! Oh, that's gonna hurt.
jokes.setup: Fair game booth at the STD fair
jokes.punchline: The carnival barker dramatically 'catches' syphilis from their own booth, performing a live STD crisis as fair entertainment — meta-commentary on the event's questionable execution
jokes.explanation: Fun visual/performance bit that embodies Greendale's particular brand of well-intentioned institutional dysfunction. Not the sharpest joke but the physicality (inferred from the dramatic text) makes it land as a crowd scene joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Tonight's gonna be great. I'm thinking we hit up that new place downtown, maybe grab some drinks, see where the night takes us. If you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And don't worry, I'll tell you all about it tomorrow. Every. Single. Detail.

jokes.text: Is she single? What are her likes and dislikes? / She likes hip-hop and horses. Dislikes beards and... yeah, I was done talking.
jokes.setup: Jeff spots Sabrina at the fair and immediately asks the Dean about her
jokes.punchline: The Dean begins listing Sabrina's dislikes and trails off ('...yeah, I was done talking') — implying he realized mid-sentence that he was revealing an inappropriate level of personal knowledge about his secretary
jokes.explanation: 'Yeah, I was done talking' is a good self-interruption that implies the Dean knows he's said too much. The list of specifics (hip-hop AND horses as a combination) is slightly absurd in a way that's characteristically Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm thinking of taking a lady friend to a very special place tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's great. Where are you taking her?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My bedroom.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, well that's... that's like going to a restaurant and asking to see the kitchen before you order.

jokes.text: Is it me, or are horses the most beautiful creatures? They're so majestic. / Totally. / I mean, just this morning when I was shaving and listening to the new Jay-Z, I was thinking about how I want to squeeze in a quick gallop this weekend.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just learned Sabrina likes hip-hop and horses; he immediately constructs a fake identity
jokes.punchline: Jeff's frantic cobbling together of 'shaving + Jay-Z + galloping' in one morning is transparently fabricated — the more he piles on, the more artificial it sounds
jokes.explanation: Jeff's social chameleon behavior exposed in real time. The specificity of 'new Jay-Z' and 'quick gallop' in a single morning is the tell — nobody would do both, and 'quick gallop' is funny phrasing. Strong character-specific comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is like Rocky IV, except instead of a Russian boxer, it's me versus you, and instead of the Cold War, it's about proving I'm stronger than I look.

jokes.text: Do you own a horse? / Can you ever really own a horse?
jokes.setup: Sabrina asks directly if Jeff owns a horse, putting him on the spot
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pseudo-philosophical dodge — 'Can you ever really own a horse?' — is a perfect pivot from the impossible to the existential, delivered with total smoothness
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Jeff's ability to turn an exposed lie into a philosophical non-answer is so perfectly him — it's simultaneously charming, evasive, and completely absurd. The question itself, applied to horses, becomes an accidental koan. Very high economy (seven words), extremely Jeff-specific, highly quotable. This deserves its high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I can't believe I lost! My arm... my beautiful arm... it's ruined! RUINED! I'll never arm wrestle again! This is the darkest day of my life!

jokes.text: Pierce introduces Jeff to Sabrina, claiming Jeff proved him wrong by getting a date — but Jeff just successfully hit on Sabrina by using the Dean's intel, taking about 30 seconds.
jokes.setup: Pierce had challenged Jeff's ability to get a date; Jeff just secured one while Pierce was away.
jokes.punchline: Pierce congratulates Jeff as if he'd overcome some great obstacle, not knowing Jeff used the Dean's information cheat sheet and did it in under a minute.
jokes.explanation: Decent structural payoff to the dry spell setup — Jeff getting a date immediately after Pierce's warning, via completely shallow means, is a satisfying ironic beat. Pierce's obliviousness adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh my stars! Is that a... a man's anatomy?!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, I've seen some sights in my day, but never did I think I'd be looking at the Captain's quarters!

jokes.text: Check out these condoms. All along the side it says 'Greendale'! Exclamation point, my idea.
jokes.setup: Dean is showing off the branded STD fair merchandise
jokes.punchline: 'Exclamation point, my idea' — the Dean is proud of punctuating the brand name on a condom, treating typography as his major creative contribution
jokes.explanation: The Dean's misplaced institutional pride is perfectly calibrated — his creative vision for a condom is adding an exclamation point. This sets up the later condom quality joke. Character-specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that... is that a real skeleton?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, why is it so... small?

jokes.text: Wow, me in a dune buggy. With syphilis. / This is going on the fridge.
jokes.setup: Pierce is looking at a poster/pamphlet from the STD fair featuring a person in a dune buggy
jokes.punchline: Pierce identifies with the syphilis patient in the marketing material and decides to display it at home — his complete lack of shame and his enthusiasm for seeing himself represented are both funny
jokes.explanation: 'This is going on the fridge' is a great button — the mundane domesticity of refrigerator display applied to syphilis branding is funny, and Pierce's self-identification with the dune buggy rider is perfectly oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Does size matter?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Of course it does.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, it absolutely doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: ...Okay, that's not helpful.

jokes.text: You wing man me, I wing man you. Maybe we split up for a little hoo-ha. And then meet in the morning for eggs and... details.
jokes.setup: Pierce lays out his plan for the double date at the STD fair
jokes.punchline: 'Eggs and... details' — the pause before 'details' implies he wants a graphic morning debrief; the entire speech is delivered as a locker room pep talk by a 70-year-old man
jokes.explanation: Pierce performing fratty bro-speak at his age is a reliable comedic mode. The 'details' beat is funny but slightly predictable. 'Hoo-ha' is a great vintage slang choice.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that the scene from Porky's?

jokes.text: That sounds like the worst combination plate ever.
jokes.setup: Pierce pitches his wingman/split up/eggs-and-details double date plan
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes Pierce's plan as a terrible restaurant order — 'combination plate' — perfectly capturing its squalid, transactional nature
jokes.explanation: Very good line. The 'combination plate' metaphor is unexpected and precise — it captures both the menu-ordering nature of Pierce's plan and its assembly of unappetizing components. Jeff's deadpan disgust lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Doreen speaks French, you know. She's très sophistiqué. I heard her say 'bonjoor' and 'mercy buckets' just yesterday.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed arm wrestling at the STD fair — escalating into a full dramatic competition with musical accompaniment
jokes.setup: Troy is upset about losing games to Abed; they begin arm wrestling at the fair
jokes.punchline: What begins as a sporting contest escalates — Troy demands a 'more inspiring song,' they switch music, and the whole thing becomes a cinematic event (Stallone in Over the Top reference) culminating in Abed breaking Troy's hand
jokes.explanation: The Troy/Abed subplot is primarily visual — the transcript captures the beats (Stallone reference, song change, broken hand) but the humor is heavily physical/cinematic. Good character work for both; Troy's pride and Abed's quiet competence are well-deployed. Rewatch value because the physical escalation reads better visually.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: She's really into wine. Like, REALLY into wine. I mean, this woman treats a Barefoot Pinot Grigio like it's foreplay. So I started calling her my little Fifty Shades of Ghirardelli.

jokes.text: Oh, like Stallone in Over the Top. But I'm not sure of all the rules. Don't I need a semi truck and a ten-year-old son?
jokes.setup: Troy declares they're arm wrestling; Abed recognizes the cinematic reference
jokes.punchline: Abed's correction of arm wrestling rules per Over the Top — specifically requiring a semi truck and a child — is both an accurate plot summary and a brilliantly literal way to engage with competition
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — taking a cinematic reference at face value and applying its literal logistics to reality. The specific requirements (semi truck, ten-year-old son) show actual knowledge of the film, which makes it funnier for people who know Over the Top and funnier for those who don't because of how specific the requirements are.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hey, did you guys know that if you microwave a whole egg, it explodes?

jokes.text: Uh, I want to wait for a more inspiring song. / This score isn't right. / There we go. [music change, full drama]
jokes.setup: Troy insists on appropriate musical accompaniment for arm wrestling
jokes.punchline: The scene becomes a full cinematic production because Troy treats every competition with maximum dramatic weight — the music changing completes the parody
jokes.explanation: Troy's insistence on the right soundtrack for arm wrestling is pure character comedy. 'This score isn't right' — framing an STD fair arm wrestling match as a movie that requires a proper score — is very funny and very Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need to go take a whiz.

jokes.text: You broke my hand, you bastard.
jokes.setup: Abed wins the dramatically scored arm wrestling match
jokes.punchline: Troy's aftermath — 'You broke my hand, you bastard' — is a genuinely pained accusation that lands as funny because (a) the whole thing was his idea and (b) 'bastard' from Troy is incongruously severe
jokes.explanation: Decent button for the arm-wrestling sequence. The broken hand as a consequence of Troy's manufactured drama is deserved, and 'bastard' from Troy is funny. Not transcendent but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're not wearing go-go boots.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: No, I'm not.

jokes.text: Oh yeah. Thar she blows.
jokes.setup: Britta and Annie have broken into the dean's office and are peeking at the anatomical model through the door
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'Thar she blows' — a Moby Dick whaling reference applied to a view of an anatomical model — is an absurdly literary choice for the moment, characteristic of Britta's attempts at wit
jokes.explanation: Very good line — the nautical/literary reference applied to seeing a penis model is an unexpected register choice that reveals Britta's particular brand of trying to be arch. The ambiguity (is it the size or just an expression?) adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta's smart. She reads books, she thinks about things. Sabrina... I asked her what the capital of France was and she said 'French people.'

jokes.text: Oh, boy. / Oh, I had it wroooong!
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta get a good look at the anatomical model in the dean's office
jokes.punchline: Their escalating reactions — 'Oh, boy' (Annie) → 'Oh, I had it wroooong!' (Britta) — imply the model is notably well-proportioned, but the comedy is entirely in what's NOT said
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of implication. 'Oh, I had it wroooong!' stretched out is a great delivery choice — the drawn-out vowel is doing real comedic work. The joke earns its impact through total economy; nothing explicit is said. High impact because a room full of viewers would absolutely erupt at Britta's prolonged revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Aging men just want someone to talk to.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: You're already here.

jokes.text: Is that considered large? / Yes. / No.
jokes.setup: Annie, still processing, asks the size question
jokes.punchline: Britta and Abed answer simultaneously and in total contradiction — Britta's 'Yes' (enthusiastic, experienced) vs. Abed's flat 'No' (comparative analysis?) — the disagreement is funnier than either answer
jokes.explanation: Brilliant three-word joke. The simultaneous contradiction tells us everything about both characters without a word of explanation: Britta is saying yes from experience/enthusiasm, Abed is saying no from whatever his reference database is. The structure is perfect — question, two-beat simultaneous contradiction, silence. One of the tightest jokes in the episode. Very high economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, some relationships are shallow. That's fine. Not everything has to be deep and meaningful. Take Sabrina—she thought 'Game of Thrones' was about a chess tournament.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's not shallow, that's just stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly my point.

jokes.text: What in the reverse porky's is going on here?
jokes.setup: Dean walks in on Annie and Britta in his office looking at the model
jokes.punchline: 'Reverse Porky's' — the Dean's framing of women peeping at anatomy as an inversion of the classic teen comedy — is both a film reference and reveals the Dean's intimate knowledge of the original
jokes.explanation: One of the Dean's best lines. 'Reverse Porky's' as a compound concept — a phrase that didn't exist before this line — perfectly captures the situation, is instantly understood, and reveals the Dean's pop-culture-informed approach to institutional management. High originality because it coined a new expression. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I prefer a woman who's a little immature. At least then she won't realize I'm a terrible person.

jokes.text: He was into S&M and Merlot, so we called it S&M&M.
jokes.setup: Doreen mentions a client who owned a vineyard in Napa and was into S&M
jokes.punchline: S&M + Merlot = S&M&M — the candy brand abbreviation is an accidental portmanteau that's both a wine pun and a kink joke
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever wordplay. S&M&M is a perfect portmanteau — it's compact, unexpected, and works on three levels (the kink, the wine, the candy). The fact that it's casually delivered by Doreen as simple nomenclature makes it funnier. High originality for a wordplay gag, strong economy. This is craft-forward humor.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: You're a terrible person and everyone knows it.

jokes.text: Pierce introduces Doreen: "You should hear her order wine in French. Hey, honey, say caber-net sauv-a-gong-da-nun."
jokes.setup: Pierce is boasting that his escort girlfriend is sophisticated and speaks six languages.
jokes.punchline: His demonstration of her French wine pronunciation — "caber-net sauv-a-gong-da-nun" — is so catastrophically wrong that it destroys his entire case for her sophistication, and by extension his for being with her. He doesn't notice.
jokes.explanation: "Caber-net sauv-a-gong-da-nun" is a transcendent malapropism — the specific phonetic disaster of this pronunciation requires genuine creative effort from the writers. Pierce's pride in Doreen's sophistication being displayed through his own catastrophic mispronunciation is structurally elegant. High originality and character integration — only Pierce would do this, and only the writers of Community would construct it this specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So what do you say, Doreen? How about you and me get to know each other a little better?

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: Pierce, we're done. I can't do this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: But I do have some business cards for my cousin who does great work. He's a plumber.

jokes.text: Be right back. I have to make tinkles.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Sabrina are having a seemingly adult, philosophical conversation at the double date
jokes.punchline: 'I have to make tinkles' — after talking with apparent sophistication, Sabrina uses pure baby-talk for the bathroom, undercutting the conversation's register entirely
jokes.explanation: Good deflating beat. After Jeff has been trying to have sophisticated conversation and Doreen has been talking intelligently about wine and S&M clients, Sabrina's 'make tinkles' is a perfect undercutting register shift. Sets up Jeff's subsequent reassessment.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: We can just talk if you want. Keep it platonic.

dialogue.speaker: Doreen
dialogue.line: My rate for conversation is still $300 an hour though.

jokes.text: You're smart, you're classy. You're not wearing go-go boots. / They're in the shop.
jokes.setup: Jeff admits to Doreen that she's not what he expected from an escort
jokes.punchline: Doreen's 'They're in the shop' — she accepts the backhanded compliment with total composure and explains the missing stereotype as a maintenance issue
jokes.explanation: Very sharp. Doreen's willingness to engage with the stereotype — not deny it, but explain its temporary absence — is funnier than any defensive response. 'They're in the shop' treats go-go boots as a professional tool requiring maintenance, which is a great character choice. High economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: 597? That's the code for 'Dean needs a hug.' I instituted it myself. Security never got the memo.

jokes.text: Trust me, I know girls I can converse with who are way more annoying. / I will take 'tinkles' over 'we need to talk' every time.
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining his complicated feelings about Sabrina's shallowness vs. more intellectually engaging but difficult women
jokes.punchline: 'I will take tinkles over we need to talk every time' — Jeff crystallizes his relationship philosophy in one sentence, privileging emotional simplicity over intellectual engagement
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical character writing. Jeff's hierarchy — 'tinkles' as the ideal over 'we need to talk' — is both very funny and genuinely revealing about his avoidance of emotional depth. The callback to Sabrina's baby-talk elevates it. This is good sitcom writing that serves character while landing as a great line.

jokes.text: You can do better.
jokes.setup: Jeff is apparently reflecting on Sabrina's departure; Doreen offers her assessment
jokes.punchline: An escort giving Jeff sincere relationship advice — 'You can do better' — delivered with complete authority, while she herself is on a date with Pierce, is deeply ironic
jokes.explanation: Good ironic line — the authority with which Doreen delivers it, and the inherent irony of the source, earns a smile. Three words, well deployed. The fact that she said it about Sabrina while dating Pierce adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Did someone just say 'penis'? In my school? We don't use that kind of language here. This is a place of learning and respect. I'm going to have to ask everyone to watch their vocabulary. From now on, we refer to male genitalia as 'the area formerly known as Prince.'

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And I'm instituting a new policy: anyone caught using anatomically correct terminology will be sentenced to a semester of mime class. Silent. Just like the genitalia itself.

jokes.text: Is there any lovemaking on the table? / We're through, Pierce. / I'm gonna go to the bar, and you can join me if you'd like. And we can still have a lovely evening. But it will cost you 200 bucks.
jokes.setup: Pierce awkwardly asks Doreen about the terms of their evening
jokes.punchline: Doreen's professional pivot — she doesn't storm off but offers a modified arrangement with a price point — is both pragmatic and funny in its matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Doreen's professionalism in restructuring the evening as a service arrangement is a good joke about the transactional nature of her work, delivered without edge. The $200 figure is specific enough to be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, let's all say it together to remove the stigma. One, two, three...

dialogue.speaker: Group
dialogue.line: Penis!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, you didn't say it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I... I was going to, but then everyone said it at the same time and I just... couldn't.

jokes.text: That is a pretty big discount.
jokes.setup: Doreen says the bar portion will cost Pierce 200 dollars
jokes.punchline: Pierce's instant calculation that this represents a 'pretty big discount' implies he already knows what her standard rate is — confirming everything about their relationship
jokes.explanation: Very economical character bomb. Pierce's quick arithmetic ('big discount') tells us he has memorized Doreen's standard rates, which tells us everything about how this relationship works. The delivery — matter-of-fact, almost impressed — makes it funnier. This is a one-sentence character reveal. High marks for structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about what you said in our last session. And I want you to know that I genuinely appreciate the breakthrough we've had together.

jokes.text: I had no idea alcohol would make people horny. Makes me sleepy. I don't...
jokes.setup: Dean is surveying the fair and observing its unintended effects
jokes.punchline: The Dean's declaration that he had 'no idea' alcohol caused arousal — immediately followed by sharing that it makes him sleepy — is a double reveal: he's oblivious to common knowledge and overshares his personal response
jokes.explanation: Good Dean line. His obliviousness about basic human behavior (combined with unsolicited personal information) is well-deployed. The 'I don't...' trailing off implies he's about to share more before stopping himself.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm perfectly comfortable with my sexuality. I'm just... not comfortable talking about it, thinking about it, or acknowledging it exists.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But I'm very comfortable being uncomfortable about it.

jokes.text: We have a 597 currently going on in your office. / A 597? / There's a dog-fighting ring in my office?
jokes.setup: Security uses a code number to report the break-in situation
jokes.punchline: The Dean's instant interpretation is 'dog-fighting ring' — his mental lexicon of emergency codes maps a peeping incident onto the most dramatic and unrelated possible crime
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection/absurdist beat. 'Dog-fighting ring' is specific enough to be funny — not just 'robbery' or 'murder,' but an exotic felony. The Dean's confident wrong answer is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I mean, it's just a wrinkly tube with a brain the size of a chickpea.

jokes.text: Okay, ladies, I am shocked at the reverse porky's that has happened here tonight.
jokes.setup: Dean addresses Annie and Britta after catching them in his office
jokes.punchline: Calling back 'reverse Porky's' — now institutionalized as the official terminology — while affecting official shock, while still clearly finding the whole thing amusing
jokes.explanation: Good callback that solidifies the coinage. The Dean using his own freshly minted phrase in official capacity is funny — it's now part of the institutional record. The studied shock is characteristically performative.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not a professor.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: You're old and you go to Greendale. That makes you a professor.

jokes.text: That's exactly why I wanted Gail, our school counselor, here, and Monique, who's keeping record, to ensure we discuss these sensitive topics in a legally appropriate manner.
jokes.setup: Annie explains Annie just needed to look at the model
jokes.punchline: The Dean has pre-assembled a school counselor AND a stenographer just to discuss the penis model situation — an absurdly over-prepared institutional response
jokes.explanation: The logistics of Gail and Monique's presence suggests the Dean anticipated exactly this scenario and was legally prepared — implying this has happened before. Good institutional absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: You're a student here?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Sabrina
dialogue.line: That's so hot.

jokes.text: I think everyone should say penis so we can take away the negative power of the word. / Penis. / She didn't say it.
jokes.setup: Gail the counselor proposes desensitization therapy via collective word-use
jokes.punchline: The group complies, but the Dean immediately focuses on Annie's non-compliance — 'She didn't say it' — with more urgency than the exercise warrants, suggesting it's become a power game
jokes.explanation: Good scene mechanics. The Dean tattling 'She didn't say it' is funnier than the exercise itself — it turns a therapeutic moment into a compliance enforcement issue. The earnestness of Gail and the opportunism of the Dean play well together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm giving up my car.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Finally, I'm free! No more car payments, no more insurance, no more—wait, what have I done?

jokes.text: Now, why did you break in to see the penis? / Wow, I really do feel more comfortable saying that now, Gail. / I just want to focus on the girl who won't say penis.
jokes.setup: Dean begins official questioning
jokes.punchline: The Dean immediately congratulates himself on therapeutic progress ('I really do feel more comfortable') then immediately pivots to pressuring Annie — using his new comfort as a weapon
jokes.explanation: Very Dean. His self-congratulation followed by immediate weaponization of his comfort against Annie is a perfect character beat — he's simultaneously genuinely participating in the exercise and using it as leverage. Good irony.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh no, the condoms are damaged from the printing process!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you mean we just had a water balloon fight with broken condoms?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm afraid so. The heat from the printer compromised the structural integrity.

jokes.text: I don't want to express myself. I don't want to sit in a room full of people and say the 'p' word. I like being repressed. I am totally comfortable being uncomfortable with my sexuality. And maybe, just maybe, if everyone were a little bit more like me, we wouldn't have to have an STD fair.
jokes.setup: Everyone is pushing Annie to 'express herself' about the penis situation
jokes.punchline: Annie's defiant speech — culminating in 'if everyone were a little more like me, we wouldn't have to have an STD fair' — is both a genuine character statement and a funny logical overcorrection
jokes.explanation: One of Annie's best speeches. 'I am totally comfortable being uncomfortable with my sexuality' is a brilliantly constructed paradox that's also genuinely philosophically defensible — AND funny. The escalation to 'we wouldn't have to have an STD fair' is perfect logic that's simultaneously absurd and correct. Very high character integration: this is entirely Annie's voice, worldview, and defensiveness. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I can't run for best athlete. I lost a footrace to Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Abed? How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: He took a shortcut through the library. I didn't know we were allowed to do that.

jokes.text: You go, girl! / That's my pumpkin!
jokes.setup: Annie delivers her defiant speech about being comfortably repressed
jokes.punchline: Shirley and Pierce's simultaneous enthusiastic endorsements — 'You go, girl!' and 'That's my pumpkin!' — from the two most unexpected corners of the group both validate Annie for different wrong reasons
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble button. Shirley's feminist solidarity and Pierce's paternal pride both land on the same beat for completely different reasons. 'That's my pumpkin!' from Pierce is especially funny — his bizarre term of endearment and the inappropriateness of claiming Annie is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Because I'm tired of being the guy who cares the most. I'm tired of wanting it more than everyone else. I just wanted to be the best at something, you know? Just once.

jokes.text: By the way, now that I've gotten a good look at one, I don't see what all the fuss was about. A giant thumb in a turtleneck. Whoop-dee-do!
jokes.setup: Annie has just made her impassioned speech about not needing to look at penises; this is immediately contradicted by her casual anatomical assessment
jokes.punchline: 'A giant thumb in a turtleneck. Whoop-dee-do!' — Annie's confident, clinical, deeply idiosyncratic description lands as the best punchline the episode's been building toward
jokes.explanation: The episode's crown jewel. 'A giant thumb in a turtleneck' is an extraordinary euphemism — specific, visual, accurate in a deeply clinical way, and utterly unlike anything anyone has said before. It works because it's genuinely Annie: she finally looked, she assessed, and her verdict is total deflation. The 'Whoop-dee-do!' caps it with her characteristic chipper dismissiveness. This is the payoff for the entire Annie subplot — built through the dean's 'Jimmy Carter,' the banana debate, breaking into the office, refusing to say the word — and the punchline earns every bit of that setup. Near-perfect scores across the board. This is what a 9.5 craft score looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to warn the students immediately about the faulty condoms in the bookstore. This is a serious health matter.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm going to send out an emergency email saying students should cease all... reproductive relations until we sort this out.

jokes.text: You have a really awesome body. / You probably hear that all the time. / Not as much as I should.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes what sounds like a standard compliment to Sabrina
jokes.punchline: Sabrina's 'Not as much as I should' — correcting the implied frequency upward, with complete lack of self-awareness — is delivered as simple fact
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the expected 'Oh, stop it.' Sabrina's correction implies she has a precise internal metric for how often she should be complimented and reality is falling short. Nicely economic, good character establishment for Sabrina.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know I've been different lately. More considerate, more willing to help people without expecting anything in return.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But I want to be clear: this is not personal growth. This is Greendale's fault.

jokes.text: But you're at Greendale... And you're old. / I'm a student. / Yikers. / Yeah, it's pretty much Yikers for me too.
jokes.setup: An older male student at the fair flirts with Sabrina; she assumes he's a professor
jokes.punchline: He's just an older student — 'Yikers' captures both the awkwardness of her assumption and the indignity of being so old at community college that you're mistaken for faculty; his 'Yeah, it's pretty much Yikers for me too' is a great mutual moment of resigned embarrassment
jokes.explanation: 'Yikers' as the word choice is funny — it's slightly archaic and dramatically insufficient for the situation. The mutual 'Yikers' acknowledgment between both characters is a sweet, funny shared beat. Good Greendale-specific joke about the demographic realities of community college.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, settling down is like a good suit. At first, you think you want something flashy, something that makes a statement. But eventually, you realize what you really need is something that fits well, keeps you warm, and doesn't make people question your judgment at the grocery store.

jokes.text: Well, I guess I can make an exception... professor.
jokes.setup: Sabrina has just said 'Yikers' about the man being a student; he confirms it's Yikers for him too
jokes.punchline: Despite the confirmed awkwardness, Sabrina decides to proceed anyway — calling him 'professor' anyway as an affectionate/ironic reclamation of the misunderstanding
jokes.explanation: Good button for the Sabrina-older-student subplot. She leans into the wrong designation anyway, suggesting her standards are situational and her social filters are loose. Decent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wow, Pierce. That was actually really mature and thoughtful.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I do have my moments.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, what, once every six months?

jokes.text: I can't do this. / What? / But this is your car. / Keep it.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Sabrina are apparently in his car about to hook up
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Keep it' in response to 'But this is your car' — he's so committed to escaping the situation that he surrenders his car rather than have sex with Sabrina
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. 'Keep it' is the perfect response — not 'it's okay, I'll walk' or any softening, just a clean transfer of property. The fact that Jeff would give away his car rather than have sex reveals how thoroughly the episode has evolved him. Very economical, strong structure, great character payoff for his arc.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking. Maybe I should stop objectifying women and start treating them with respect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wow, Pierce, that's actually really mature.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... how much would that cost me?

jokes.text: Yeah! Yes! / Yes! / How you like those apples? / I don't like those apples. I'm so upset.
jokes.setup: Troy has finally beaten Abed at something (a fair game, inferred from context)
jokes.punchline: Abed's completely flat 'I don't like those apples. I'm so upset' — delivered as pure information, not genuine emotion — parodies the emotional response Troy wanted from him
jokes.explanation: One of Abed's best moments. 'I don't like those apples. I'm so upset.' delivered as a flat statement of announced feelings — not felt feelings — is perfect Abed. He's narrating what upset looks like rather than experiencing it. Very high character integration. The contrast with Troy's genuine excitement is the comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, back in my day, I used to pay for all kinds of—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, I will literally pay you money right now to not finish that sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Done.

jokes.text: Wow, this may be the only STD fair to actually spread STDs.
jokes.setup: Chaos has broken out at the fair — condom water balloons are being thrown
jokes.punchline: The meta-observation that the awareness fair has become the vector it was designed to prevent
jokes.explanation: Sharp one-liner that perfectly encapsulates the episode's comedic thesis about Greendale's institutional dysfunction. The irony is clean and well-structured. Ben the security guard as the voice of reason is good casting for this observation.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Attention students: due to a manufacturing defect, all condoms in the campus health center have been recalled. Please do not use them.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's right, go ahead. Live a little.

jokes.text: Dude, these are leaking. / Oh, my God. That's why you don't print things on condoms.
jokes.setup: Students in a condom water balloon fight discover the condoms are defective
jokes.punchline: The Dean's instant analysis — 'that's why you don't print things on condoms' — treats this as a known rule he violated rather than a catastrophe he caused
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. The Dean framing his own mistake as a general principle ('that's why you don't...') implies this is received wisdom he ignored — the confidence with which he identifies his own error as a learning opportunity is very Dean. The 'Exclamation point, my idea' callback makes this land harder.

jokes.text: Condom water balloon fight — visual scene of Greendale students engaged in a water balloon fight with promotional condoms
jokes.setup: The STD fair has condom water balloons as part of the festivities.
jokes.punchline: The STD awareness event devolves into gleeful chaos with branded condom water balloons. The image of people getting soaked by condom-balloon water at a health fair is inherently absurd.
jokes.explanation: A mostly visual gag whose comedy comes from the escalation of the fair's dysfunction. Works well on screen and completes the institutional collapse arc. Limited quotability but strong visual impact.

jokes.text: Everyone's getting preggers, and it's all your fault.
jokes.setup: The faulty condoms have been used in a water balloon fight
jokes.punchline: The accusation of causing mass pregnancy via a water balloon fight — using 'preggers' in the same breath as a serious accusation — condenses the whole absurdity
jokes.explanation: Decent line. 'Preggers' is a funny word choice that undercuts the severity. The accusation's logic is comically flawed (water balloon fight ≠ pregnancy risk) but everyone acts as if it's real, which is the joke.

jokes.text: "Oh, God, I love it." [Dean reacts to the condom water balloon chaos]
jokes.setup: The STD fair has collapsed into a condom-balloon fight that will almost certainly spread STDs.
jokes.punchline: The Dean's immediate pivot from administrative crisis to genuine delight — "Oh, God, I love it" — reveals that institutional chaos brings him joy. His instinct is never to fix problems but to appreciate their spectacle.
jokes.explanation: A quick Dean character beat that's perfectly economical. His joy at institutional disaster is a consistent character trait — he's never the solution, always the appreciative audience. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Troy, all the condoms are faulty. As the best athlete on campus, I need you to run to my office and make an announcement.
jokes.setup: Dean needs someone to run across campus quickly
jokes.punchline: His basis for choosing Troy — 'best athlete on campus' — is both flattering and immediately about to be contradicted, and his urgent task is an announcement about not using the free condoms he just gave everyone
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the Troy/Abed reveal below. Functional but its value is in what it enables, not in itself.

jokes.text: Dean, I am not the best athlete on campus. / Abed is. / I know you let me win the race. / But you didn't say anything. / That's because... I wanted it to be true.
jokes.setup: Troy is asked to run as the best athlete; he immediately reveals the truth about their earlier race
jokes.punchline: 'That's because... I wanted it to be true' — Troy's reason for not correcting Abed is an unexpectedly tender admission of insecurity from the show's most athletically confident character
jokes.explanation: Excellent emotional punchline. The Troy/Abed subplot — set up through the basketball challenge, the arm wrestling, the race — pays off here with something genuinely touching. 'I wanted it to be true' is funny AND moving, which is Community's highest achievement. It recontextualizes Troy's competitive behavior throughout the episode as wounded pride rather than arrogance. Very high character integration and earned vs. cheap scores.

jokes.text: You're a really good friend. / No, Abed... / You are.
jokes.setup: Troy calls Abed a good friend after the emotional revelation
jokes.punchline: Troy sets up to redirect the compliment back to Abed with 'No, Abed...' pause — but Abed cuts him off with 'You are,' stealing the reversal before Troy can deliver it
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic structure. The classic 'no, YOU are' exchange is a cliché — but Abed delivers his half before Troy can complete the setup, cutting off the sentimental beat with his own version of it. It's simultaneously sweet, meta-aware, and very Abed (he saw the structure coming and completed it efficiently). One of the episode's highest craft moments. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: For the love of God, run! / Okay. / Go, Abed, go, before people sex one another!
jokes.setup: Abed is dispatched to make the announcement about the faulty condoms
jokes.punchline: 'Before people sex one another!' — the Dean's desperate rephrasing uses 'sex' as a verb in its most panicked and unglamorous form
jokes.explanation: 'Sex one another' as a verb construction is funny — it treats sexual activity as an action being done TO each other rather than with, implying chaos rather than consent. The Dean's escalating alarm is well-deployed.

jokes.text: Oh, it's not Greendale, Jeff, it's you. You're becoming more mature. I mean, a man reaches a point in his life where he stops looking for a place to hang his underwear and starts looking for a place to hang his hat.
jokes.setup: Jeff confesses that something stopped him from going through with Sabrina — attributing it to Greendale
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers what sounds like wisdom but the metaphor ('hang his underwear' → 'hang his hat') is delivered by a man who just paid an escort for a reduced-rate evening — the source makes the wisdom absurd
jokes.explanation: Pierce accidentally delivers real wisdom while being deeply unqualified to do so — the metaphor itself is decent, but the irony of its source is the main joke. The 'hang his underwear' phrasing is nicely crude as the lower-aspiration option.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I was waiting for that to become inappropriate or racist.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just delivered a surprisingly decent piece of life advice
jokes.punchline: Jeff admits he was listening for the other shoe to drop — his expectation of Pierce's racism/inappropriateness is so trained that genuine wisdom from Pierce surprises him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most self-aware jokes. It's both a meta-comment on Pierce as a character (and on the show's use of him) and a genuine character beat for Jeff acknowledging the relationship dynamic. The word 'racist' is used clinically and correctly. Very quotable, strong character integration for both Jeff AND Pierce.

jokes.text: Oh, uh, she said if I wanted to continue the night I'd have to pay. / Oh, man, that... that is rough. / Oh, no, it was a wake-up call. Doreen's a very special lady. I did not treat her right. I have stuff to work on, you know?
jokes.setup: Jeff asks what happened with Doreen
jokes.punchline: Pierce treats being charged by his escort as a moment of spiritual clarity — reframing commercial sex as a relationship he failed — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Pierce's sincere self-reflection about 'not treating Doreen right' — when their relationship is entirely transactional — applies relationship guilt to a commercial transaction in a way that's both sad and funny. 'I have stuff to work on' from Pierce is delivered as genuine growth, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Here's to being better men. / Cheers. / So could I borrow 200 bucks?
jokes.setup: Jeff and Pierce share a sincere toast to self-improvement
jokes.punchline: Pierce immediately follows 'Here's to being better men' with a request for money to pay Doreen — the warm moment is instantly monetized
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button with real wit. The juxtaposition of the sincere toast and the immediate transaction request is satisfying — Pierce's growth is entirely abstract while his needs are very concrete. The structure (toast → beat → request) is crisp.

jokes.text: Tell Doreen I say hi.
jokes.setup: Pierce has gone to pay Doreen with Jeff's money
jokes.punchline: Jeff's parting shot — 'Tell Doreen I say hi' — treats this absurd arrangement with complete social normalcy, as if Pierce is going to visit a mutual acquaintance
jokes.explanation: Very economical button. 'Tell Doreen I say hi' normalizes the whole situation with five words. Jeff extending social niceties to an escort he just met through Pierce is perfectly dry. Almost perfect economy.

jokes.text: You know, for 220 I can get the... / I'll give you 250 if you don't finish telling me.
jokes.setup: Pierce begins describing what additional services $220 gets from Doreen
jokes.punchline: Jeff offers $250 for Pierce to stop — paying a premium for the privilege of ignorance, valuing not knowing over money
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The economic logic — Jeff paying more to hear less — perfectly captures his relationship with Pierce's oversharing. The beat structure (Pierce begins the revelation, Jeff's offer cuts him off) is tight. 'If you don't finish telling me' is a brilliantly inverted transaction. Very high marks across the board.

jokes.text: Ooh, I can get it twice.
jokes.setup: Jeff offers Pierce $250 to stop talking
jokes.punchline: Pierce's instant calculation that $250 is enough to get the service twice — confirming his standard rate while completely missing Jeff's point
jokes.explanation: Perfect button. Pierce's arithmetic — $250 buys it twice at Doreen's rate — is simultaneously a callback to the pricing structure and a demonstration of his complete inability to hear subtext. His enthusiasm ('Ooh') while mentally calculating escort rates is pure Pierce. The economy is extraordinary for such a character-rich beat.

jokes.text: Ah, college. Best years of our lives.
jokes.setup: Pierce gleefully runs off with Jeff's $250 to pay an escort at a faulty-condom STD fair
jokes.punchline: Jeff's completely flat 'Ah, college. Best years of our lives.' — the most clichéd sentiment applied to the most undignified situation
jokes.explanation: Good final button for the Pierce/Jeff plot. The cliché lands with perfect irony given everything that's just happened. Jeff's embrace of the platitude as a coping mechanism is very character-appropriate. Good closing beat.

jokes.text: Attention, Greendale students. Don't use the condoms! If you're going to have sex tonight, don't use condoms.
jokes.setup: Abed has been sent to announce that the condoms are faulty and shouldn't be used
jokes.punchline: Abed's literalist PA announcement — 'If you're going to have sex tonight, don't use condoms' — strips all context, making it sound like a pro-unprotected-sex message rather than a product recall
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. Abed's literal interpretation of 'announce that the condoms are bad, don't use them' removes all context and produces the worst possible public health announcement. 'If you're going to have sex tonight, don't use condoms' is the exact opposite of STD fair messaging — delivered by Abed with complete matter-of-fact authority. Very high character integration (only Abed would strip the context this precisely), great callback payoff, and the perfect dark ironic closing beat for an STD awareness episode. One of the episode's top moments.

tmdb_overview: With his high-price "escort" girlfriend on his arm, Pierce pressures Jeff into asking Dean Pelton's airhead secretary to double date at the STD Fair.
insight: Sex ed debate spawns 76 jokes in 22 minutes—Jeff's deflection carries the episode.
